# subject: ENG-205
# topic: Midsummer Acts 3–4
# title: ENG-205 Midsummer Acts 3–4 — 5 Examples (quotes)
# short: 5 Examples (quotes)
# order: 5
# expect: 14
Bless thee, Bottom! bless thee! thou art translated.
column2: Peter Quince says this in 3.1.60 when Bottom re-enters with an ass's head, using "translated" to mean changed or transformed.

column1: What angel wakes me from my flowery bed?
column2: Titania, still under Oberon's love-juice, says this in 3.1.65 as she wakes to Bottom's singing.

column1: reason and love keep little company together now-a-days
column2: Bottom says this in 3.1.70 after Titania swears she loves him, joking that reason and love are now strangers.

column1: My mistress with a monster is in love.
column2: Puck reports this to Oberon in 3.2.10 after leaving Bottom "translated" for Titania to see when she wakes.

column1: This is the woman; but not this the man.
column2: Puck says this in 3.2.45 when Demetrius and Hermia enter, showing Oberon that Puck anointed the wrong Athenian.

column1: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
column2: Puck says this in 3.2.120 as he and Oberon stand aside to watch Lysander plead with Helena.

column1: O Helen! goddess, nymph, perfect, divine!
column2: Demetrius says this in 3.2.144 when he wakes after Oberon has charmed his eyes, instantly doting on Helena.

column1: And though she be but little, she is fierce.
column2: Helena says this of Hermia in 3.2.343, after calling her a vixen at school, which Hermia hears as another insult about her height.

column1: Jack shall have Jill; / Nought shall go ill.
column2: Puck recites this country proverb in 3.2.490-494 as he squeezes the remedy onto Lysander's eyes so each man will wake to his own love.

column1: Dian's bud o'er Cupid's flower / Hath such force and blessed power.
column2: Oberon says this in 4.1.55-58 as he touches Titania's eyes with an herb to undo the love-juice and release her from Bottom.

column1: Methought I was enamour'd of an ass.
column2: Titania says this in 4.1.60 when she wakes, then loathes Bottom's visage once the spell is lifted.

column1: Egeus, I will overbear your will.
column2: Theseus says this in 4.1.165 after Demetrius declares his love for Helena, ruling that the three couples shall be married in the temple.

column1: it shall be called 'Bottom's Dream,' because it hath no bottom
column2: Bottom, waking in 4.1, plans this ballad of a vision "past the wit of man to say," mixing the senses as he tries to report it.

column1: You must say, 'paragon:' a paramour is, God bless us! a thing of naught.
column2: Flute corrects Quince in 4.2 after Quince praises Bottom's voice with the wrong word, "paramour."
